sentence: Hepatitis C is an infection with a virus that causes inflammation of the liver, which can damage the liver over time.
note: NHS Highland: hepatitis C causes inflammation of the liver, and the inflamed organ can become damaged over time. Search summary blended with nhs.uk page.

sentence: Hepatitis C is a virus that causes inflammation of the liver, and over time the inflamed liver can become damaged.
Most people with hepatitis C have no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it.
note: NHS and MedlinePlus: most people have no symptoms.

sentence: It is spread through contact with infected blood.
note: WHO: spread through contact with infected blood.

sentence: It is diagnosed with a blood test, and treatment is a short course of antiviral tablets.
note: NHS Highland: simple blood test; short course of antiviral tablets.

sentence: Without treatment it can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
note: MedlinePlus and NHS Highland list cirrhosis, liver failure, liver cancer.

sentence: Hepatitis C is caused by a virus that is spread through contact with infected blood.
note: WHO: spread through contact with infected blood.

sentence: Casual contact does not spread the virus, and it is not passed on through breast milk, food or water, according to WHO.
note: WHO as summarised by the search.

sentence: Sharing drug-injecting equipment.
note: NHS lists sharing injecting equipment as a risk.

sentence: Having medical care abroad, in a part of the world where hepatitis C is more common.
note: NHS lists medical care abroad / high-prevalence areas.

sentence: Having received certain blood transfusions or transplants in the UK in the past.
note: NHS lists certain transfusions or transplants in the UK; cut-off dates differed between NHS pages so none are given.

sentence: Being the baby of a mother who has hepatitis C.
note: NHS lists babies of infected mothers.

sentence: Having a tattoo abroad.
note: British Liver Trust urges testing after a tattoo abroad.

sentence: Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice) may be seen.
Swelling of the tummy from fluid may occur.
note: MedlinePlus lists abdominal swelling from fluid.

sentence: Cirrhosis, which is scarring of the liver.
note: NHS: untreated infection can eventually cause scarring (cirrhosis).

sentence: Liver failure.
Liver cancer.
The risk of liver damage rises with regular alcohol use or infection with hepatitis B or HIV.
note: MedlinePlus: risk rises with regular alcohol use or co-infection with hepatitis B or HIV.

sentence: Hepatitis C is diagnosed using two blood tests, an antibody test and a PCR test.
note: NHS diagnosis page: 2 blood tests, antibody and PCR.

sentence: The antibody test shows past exposure, while a positive PCR test means the infection is current.
note: NHS and British Liver Trust: positive antibody test followed by RNA/PCR to confirm active infection.

sentence: Tests are available through GPs, sexual health clinics and drug treatment services.
note: NHS pages list these places (blended summary).

sentence: Treatment is with antiviral medicines.
note: NHS/MedlinePlus: treatment is with antiviral medicines.

sentence: The medicines now used are tablets called direct-acting antivirals, taken daily for 8 to 12 weeks, according to the British Liver Trust.
note: BLT: DAAs are tablets, every day, for 8 to 12 weeks.

sentence: A specialist usually manages treatment.
note: MedlinePlus: usually a specialist manages treatment.

sentence: There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.
Ways to reduce the risk include not sharing drug-injecting equipment, razors or toothbrushes.
note: NHS (blended search summary) and UK guidance for GPs.

sentence: The NHS advises a GP appointment for anyone who has symptoms or thinks they could have been infected.
note: NHS: see a GP if you have symptoms or think you could have been infected.

sentence: The British Liver Trust urges testing for anyone who has ever injected drugs, had a tattoo abroad or had unprotected sex with someone who may have been infected, even if they feel well.
note: BLT stresses testing for these groups even when well.

sentence: Most people with hepatitis C have no symptoms.
Because of this, many people do not know they have the virus.
note: NHS Highland: symptoms often absent so many people do not know.

sentence: When symptoms do appear, they can take weeks, months or even years to start.
note: NHS: symptoms can take weeks, months or years.

sentence: Early symptoms can include a high temperature, tiredness, tummy pain, loss of appetite, feeling or being sick, and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, which is called jaundice.
Among people who get early symptoms, around 1 in 5 have jaundice.
MedlinePlus also lists itching, dark urine and pale, clay-coloured stools as possible symptoms.
It lists swelling of the tummy caused by fluid as well.
The British Liver Trust says symptoms are often vague, such as tiredness or loss of appetite, and can be mistaken for other conditions.
It adds that about 8 in 10 people with a new, or acute, infection have no symptoms.
For longer-lasting infection, the Trust lists tiredness, itchy skin, nausea, joint pain and mood changes among the possible symptoms.
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with infected blood.
The NHS lists sharing drug-injecting equipment as a risk.
It also lists having medical care abroad, and some blood transfusions or transplants in the UK in the past.
A baby can catch the virus from an infected mother, and UK guidance describes this as uncommon.
note: NHS lists babies of infected mothers; UK guidance in search summary called it uncommon. Blended.

sentence: The NHS describes sexual transmission as very rare.
WHO says casual contact does not spread the virus.
It is also not passed on through breast milk, food or water.
UK guidance suggests not sharing razors or toothbrushes.
The British Liver Trust urges testing for anyone who has ever injected drugs or had a tattoo abroad, even if they feel well.
Because the virus can be present for years without symptoms, testing is the only way to know whether someone has it.
note: NHS: symptoms can take years; BLT/NHS: diagnosed by blood tests. Mild inference from both.

sentence: Hepatitis C is diagnosed with a blood test.
Two blood tests are used, an antibody test and a PCR test.
The antibody test shows that a person has been exposed to the virus at some point.
A positive PCR test means the infection is current.
The British Liver Trust says a positive antibody test is followed by an RNA test to confirm active infection.
Tests are available from GPs, sexual health clinics, genitourinary medicine clinics and drug treatment services.
NHS England also offers a free, confidential home test kit that people aged 18 or over in England can order online.
The kit uses a finger-prick blood sample that is posted to a laboratory.
note: Search summary of NHS England page.

sentence: Testing is suggested even without symptoms, because many people feel well.
Anyone diagnosed is usually referred to a specialist for treatment.
note: MedlinePlus: usually a specialist manages treatment.

sentence: Hepatitis C is treated with antiviral medicines.
The medicines now used are called direct-acting antivirals.
They are tablets taken every day for 8 to 12 weeks, the British Liver Trust says.
NHS England describes treatment as a short course of antiviral tablets that clears the virus in more than 95 in 100 cases.
note: NHS England release as summarised; date/figure from search summary, not full page.

sentence: WHO reports that direct-acting antivirals can clear the virus in more than 95 in 100 people.
The British Liver Trust says more than 9 in 10 people get rid of the virus with treatment.
Most people have no side effects, and headache and tiredness are the most common ones when they happen.
Interferon, the older treatment, is no longer used for hepatitis C in the UK.
A specialist usually manages treatment.
With a new infection, a clinician may wait to see whether it becomes long-lasting before starting treatment.
note: MedlinePlus: provider may wait to see if infection becomes chronic.

sentence: In about 1 in 4 people the immune system clears the virus within a few months.
In the others the infection stays for years, which is called chronic hepatitis C.
Without treatment, it can eventually cause scarring of the liver, called cirrhosis.
MedlinePlus says untreated hepatitis C may also lead to liver failure and liver cancer.
The risk of liver damage rises with regular alcohol use or infection with hepatitis B or HIV.
Catching hepatitis C again is possible, and completing treatment does not make a person immune.
Clearing the virus, whether naturally or through treatment, does not give lasting protection.
note: Search summary of UK guidance on reinfection; blended.

sentence: The British Liver Trust advises people who are recovering to keep alcohol to a very small amount.
It says a doctor may advise no alcohol at all if liver damage is more severe.
NHS England is aiming to eliminate hepatitis C as a public health threat, with a target of 2030.
note: Search summary of NHS England pages.
